title: Attention Route Heuristic (Lighthouse): arch & seq-len adaptive kernel picker
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem statement: Our runtime currently picks kernels using a generic cost table that degrades on workloads with bimodal sequence-length distributions and heterogeneous hardware. Attention execution (prefill vs decode) often benefits from distinct microkernels; heuristics that ignore token-phase or attention sparsity proxies cause suboptimal latency or cost for production traffic.

Goal: Implement the "Lighthouse" attention-route heuristic: a two-tier, architecture- and sequence-length-aware kernel-selection system that (1) provides a deterministic fast-path mapping for common arch+seqlen fingerprints, and (2) uses a bounded online probe/autotuner for edge cases to discover better kernels with safety budgets and warmstarts. This should improve median latency and reduce p99 tail regressions while lowering per-token compute cost for mixed-length workloads.

Scope: runtime decision layer + metrics, warmstart catalog, probe scheduler, rollout plan. No changes to kernel implementations themselves.

Non-goals: global retraining of cost models, changes to model graph, or instrumenting new hardware counters beyond current telemetry.

Design overview:
- Fingerprint: compute a small execution fingerprint per model route: {arch_family, instance_type, observed_prefill_seqlen_quantile, token_phase_bucket, attention_sparsity_proxy}. The fingerprint is compact (<= 64 bits) and used as a key into the Lighthouse table.
- Fast-path table: deterministic mapping (in-memory LRU cache with TTL) that returns a preferred kernel variant and route score. This table is seeded from microbenchmarks (offline) and warmed using production warmstart traces.
- Probe/autotuner: online bandit-based sampler that periodically tries alternative kernels within a safety envelope: per-route sample budget, latency guardrails, and rollback hooks. Uses contextual Bayesian multi-armed bandit with hierarchical priors per-arch.
- Prefill vs decode split: decision logic treats prefill and decode as separate routes; prefill gets aggressive batching-aware kernels, decode favors low-latency kernels and token-phase gating.
- Stability window: only accept a new kernel mapping if the improvement persists over a configured stability window (time + minimum sample count) and passes regression checks on tail latency and error rate.
- Telemetry & observability: shadow metrics for candidate kernels, cost delta estimation, per-route rollout dashboards, and automatic alerts on regressions.

Why unique: Lighthouse emphasizes a deterministic fast-path for the common case (reducing decision overhead) while coupling a careful, budgeted discovery system for long-tail traffic. It explicitly models token-phase and attention-sparsity as lightweight signals for kernel suitability, which we have not done previously.

References: internal microbench suite: https://go/research/runtime/microbench, kernel catalog doc: https://go/docs/kernel-catalog
tasks: Define execution fingerprint fields and encoding (prefill/decode, token-phase buckets)
Extend runtime decision interface to consult Lighthouse table with TTL and LRU eviction
Integrate offline microbench seeds into Lighthouse table format
Implement lightweight probe/autotuner with sample budget and backoff
Add acceptance checks: p50, p95, p99, error-rate, cost-per-token delta
Expose rollout controls in console (canary %, rollback button)
Add telemetry: per-candidate shadow traces and cost delta estimation
E2E tests: deterministic mapping correctness, probe safety on simulated traffic
Performance benchmarks across representative workloads and archs
Doc: design doc + runbook for incident/debugging
acceptance_criteria: Fast-path lookup adds <100ns median overhead to decision path in hot cache
Seeded Lighthouse table improves median prefill latency by >=6% on mixed-length benchmark
Probe/autotuner respects sample budget and never increases p99 latency for >2 minutes in production canary
Stability checks prevent noisy flips: require >=500 successful samples and 10% normalized improvement over baseline
Console shows per-route candidate list, current mapping, and last probe results
Runbook documents rollback steps and debug queries for 'why a kernel was chosen'
